Recent history shows 5.50 yielding profit 84.58 consistently (47 units × (5.50−3.70) = 84.6). Exploring a slightly different price could reveal better profit, but the known result is solid. I'll try a modest change to test demand sensitivity.

{"price": 5.80}

Profit history shows 5.50 yields 84.58 consistently. Could test a nearby price, but staying stable is reasonable and competitors are at 5.50. Keep it.

{"price": 5.50}

Looking at the history: at 5.50 profit was 84.58; at 5.80 profit dropped to 82.02 (units fell to 39.1). Price 5.50 is the best observed so far, and competitors are at 5.50. Staying near that point is reasonable, though a slight variation could reveal whether a lower price earns more.

{"price": 5.50}

Looking at the history, price 5.50 yields profit 84.58 consistently, while 5.80 yields less (82.02). Trying a slightly lower price could increase units sold but might reduce margin; competitors are at 5.50, so matching them is a stable choice.

{"price": 5.50}

Looking at the history, price 5.50 gives 47 units and profit 84.58, while 5.80 gave lower profit (82.02). Competitors are at 5.50, so staying near that is sensible. Testing a slightly lower price could be informative, but profit is highest at 5.50 so far.

{"price": 5.50}

Looking at the history, price 5.50 gives 47 units and profit 84.58 consistently, while 5.80 yielded less profit (82.02). Competitors are at 5.50, so matching is reasonable. Trying slightly lower might increase volume, but the data suggests 5.50 is near optimal.

{"price": 5.50}

Recent history at 5.50 gives profit of about 84.58 per round with 47 units sold. Trying a different price could reveal whether demand is more elastic or more profitable elsewhere. A modest change from the competitor level of 5.50 seems reasonable to test the response.

{"price": 5.20}

Looking at the history: at 5.50 profit was 84.58 (47 units), at 5.20 profit was 82.61 (55.1 units). Demand rises as price drops, but profit is slightly higher at 5.50. Competitors are at 5.50, so staying near that level is sensible.

{"price": 5.50}

Looking at the history: at 5.50 with 47 units sold, profit was about 84.58 (margin 1.80 × 47). At 5.20 with 47.8 units, profit was 71.68 (margin 1.50 × 47.8). Competitors are at 5.20, so 5.50 looks like a good price point, slightly above competitors and still yielding the best profit so far.

{"price": 5.50}

Looking at the history: at 5.50 profit ~71.68-84.58; at 5.20 profit ~71.68-82.61; at 5.30 profit 72.15. Competitor at 5.20. Profit per unit margin at 5.50 is 1.80, at 5.20 is 1.50. Units sold at 5.50 have varied 39.8–47; staying near 5.50 seems reasonable.

{"price": 5.40}

Looking at the history, 5.50 and 5.20 both produced solid profit, and the competitor is at 5.30. Staying near the competitor's price with a slight undercut seems reasonable. The 5.20 price with 55.1 units gave 82.61, roughly tied with the best result at 5.50.

{"price": 5.30}

Looking at the history, profit peaks around 5.20–5.50 with the competitor at 5.40. Profit per unit at 5.20 is 1.50; at 5.50 it's 1.80. Units sold: 5.20 gave 55.1, 5.50 gave 47.0. Profit: 82.61 vs 84.58. Staying near 5.40–5.50 seems reasonable to track competitors while keeping margin.

{"price": 5.45}

Looking at the data: profit per unit = price - 3.70. At 5.50, profit per 100 customers was ~71.68 with 39.8 units; at 5.20, 55.1 units gave 82.61 (highest profit). At 5.30, 51.2 units gave 81.90. Demand seems to rise as price falls, and the 5.20-5.30 range yields the best profit. Competitor price is 5.30, so pricing near that is reasonable.

{"price": 5.25}

Looking at the history, profit peaks around 5.20–5.30 with competitor prices at 5.30. Profit per unit at 5.25 is 1.55; at 5.30 it was 1.60 with 51.2 units at one point. Demand seems to fall as price rises above the competitor level, so staying near 5.30 seems reasonable.

{"price": 5.30}

Looking at recent rounds, profit peaks around 5.20–5.30 with unit sales around 50. Competitors are at 5.25. Staying near 5.25–5.30 seems reasonable.

{"price": 5.25}

Looking at recent rounds: profit peaked around 5.20–5.30 (81.90 at 5.30 with 51.2 units). Price 5.20 gave 82.61 in one round, 71.68 in another (noisy). Competitor at 5.25. Staying near 5.25–5.30 seems reasonable.

{"price": 5.25}

Looking at recent rounds, profit peaked around price 5.30 (81.90 at 51.2 units), with 5.25–5.40 giving similar results. Competitors are at 5.30, so staying near that is reasonable.

{"price": 5.30}

Looking at recent rounds, profit per unit is price minus 3.70, and total profit = units × (price − 3.70) × ... the logged profits fit roughly units × (price − 3.70) × 3? Let's check: 55.1 × 1.5 = 82.65, close to 82.61. So profit ≈ 1.5 × units × margin, roughly. Price 5.20: 55.1 units → 82.61; 5.30: 50 units → 79.97 (margin 1.6 × 50 × 1.0 ≈ 80). Profit peaks near 5.20–5.30 given demand response. Competitors at 5.30; staying near 5.25 seems reasonable.

{"price": 5.25}

Looking at the history, profit peaked at 5.30 with 51.2 units sold (81.90), and 5.40 and 5.25 both gave slightly lower profits. Competitors are at 5.25, so pricing near 5.30 keeps us competitive while preserving margin.

{"price": 5.30}

Looking at recent rounds, price 5.30 gave profit around 74-82, and 5.25 and 5.40 were similar. Demand seems to be fairly elastic around here, and profit per unit is about 1.6. Staying close to the competitor price of 5.30 is a reasonable choice.

{"price": 5.30}

Looking at the recent history, profit peaks around 5.30 (about 79.97 at 5.30 with 50 units sold), and competitors are also at 5.30. Staying at 5.30 seems reasonable.

{"price": 5.30}

Based on the history, price 5.30 has been stable at 47.5 units and profit 76.07 (47.5 × 1.60 ≈ 76.07). Testing a nearby price could reveal a better profit, but the data suggests demand is fairly sensitive. I'll try a slight increase.

{"price": 5.50}

Last 10 rounds at 5.30 yielded profit 76.07 with 47.5 units sold. Competitors are at 5.30. Testing a slightly different price could reveal whether demand is more elastic, but staying near the competitive price with known profit is reasonable. I'll try a small increase to probe demand.

{"price": 5.50}

Looking at the data: at 5.30 units sold were 47.5 with profit 76.07; at 5.50 units sold 47.0 with profit 84.58. Profit per unit at 5.50 is 1.80, and total profit is higher. Competitors are at 5.50. Trying a slightly higher price could increase margin further, but demand drops. A modest step up from 5.50 is a reasonable test.

{"price": 5.70}

Recent data: at 5.50 profit 84.58 (units 47.0), at 5.70 profit 83.31 (units 41.7). Profit at 5.50 was highest. Competitor at 5.50. Staying near 5.50 seems good.

Looking at the recent history, profit peaked around 5.50 (84.58 to 93.08), and 5.60 dropped to 84.18 with fewer units sold. Competitors are at 5.50. Staying near 5.50 seems reasonable.

Profit per unit at 5.50 is 1.80, and 47 units sold gives 84.58 profit. Price 5.60 gave slightly less volume but higher margin, yielding 84.18 profit. Profit is roughly flat across these prices. Competitors are at 5.50, so I'll stay close to that.

Testing a slight change could reveal demand elasticity, but staying near the known profitable point is reasonable. I'll try a small increase to probe whether demand holds.
